# Archival Time Research Notes

Collecting some research notes that may or may not turn into full essays

## Superhistory and Common Law

Venkatesh Rao’s idea of “superhistory” is useful because it shifts the discussion of AI away from intelligence and toward time. His argument is that artificial systems can accumulate experience at a rate biological beings cannot. A chess engine can play more games in a day than a human could in several lifetimes; an AI system can ingest more text than anyone could read in centuries. The result is not necessarily a system that is “smarter” in some general sense, but one that is experientially older. Rao calls this condition Artificial Time.

What interests me is that, once you frame the problem this way, artificial time begins to look less unprecedented. Human institutions have always tried to detach experience from the lifespan of an individual. Common law is one obvious example.

A judge deciding a case is not reasoning only from personal experience. The court inherits decisions made by people who encountered analogous disputes decades or centuries earlier. A past event becomes a case, the case becomes precedent, and the precedent alters what happens when a later event arrives. The institution is older than anyone participating in it.

Common law is not superhistory in Rao’s strong sense. It is slow, lossy and bottlenecked by human interpretation. But it does suggest an older lineage of technologies for accumulating experience outside the individual.

The important step is that common law does not simply preserve the past. It weights it. Cases do not all exert equal force. A binding precedent matters differently from persuasive authority. Jurisdiction matters, hierarchy matters, factual similarity matters. A precedent can become stronger through repeated use or weaker through distinction and neglect. Legal reasoning is therefore partly a process for deciding how much influence a past event should exercise over the present.
That distinction between traces and weights seems important. A trace records that something happened. A weight records, in effect, how much that event should change future behavior. The useful residue of touching a hot pan is not a perfect memory of the event; it is the changed disposition that follows from it. The next time your hand approaches something hot, the space of possible actions has been reorganized.

This suggests a longer spectrum:
**Custom → common law → bureaucracy/science → databases → artificial intelligence**

Each stage preserves experience in a different way, but more importantly, each develops a different system for deciding how strongly the past should bear on the future.

Custom may be the simplest case. Repetition produces weight without necessarily preserving much of the original event. A practice has been followed many times, and eventually the repetition itself becomes a reason to continue it.

Common law makes weighting more explicit by attaching different levels of authority to recorded cases. Bureaucracy moves experience into files, categories and procedures, allowing organizations to retain information after the people who produced it have left. Science develops still more elaborate weighting systems: replication, sample size, confidence, methodology, citation. A result matters not simply because it occurred, but because institutions have ways of determining how much epistemic weight it should carry.

The database changes the problem. Once storage becomes cheap, institutions no longer have to discard nearly as much. Huge numbers of traces can simply be retained. But storage alone is not experience. A database containing a billion events has not necessarily learned anything from them. It preserves history without yet deciding what in that history matters.

Artificial intelligence changes the relationship again. AI systems can take large numbers of traces and convert them into dispositions toward future situations. The past is no longer stored only as a retrievable archive; some residue of it is incorporated into how the system responds. In contemporary AI, the language of “weights” is strikingly apt. What a system has encountered becomes differential influence over what it will do next.

That gives us a simple distinction. An archive preserves traces. Experience weights traces. Artificial Time accelerates the conversion of traces into weights.

Seen this way, the novelty of AI is not simply that it has access to more history. Humans have had archives, libraries and bureaucracies for a long time. The novelty is that artificial systems can potentially turn enormous amounts of recorded or simulated experience into new dispositions without waiting for chronological time to pass.
Human expertise is slow because experience is coupled to life. A doctor has to encounter patients over years. A judge has to see cases. An engineer has to watch systems fail. Institutions partially solve this problem by allowing the experience of others to survive in precedents, records and procedures. Artificial intelligence pushes the same project much further by allowing vastly more encounters to be processed and incorporated than any individual could experience directly.
This makes superhistory look less like the arrival of an entirely new kind of intelligence and more like the latest stage in a much older effort to make the past operational. Custom, law, bureaucracy, science and artificial intelligence all provide ways for previous events to shape future action without requiring each individual to live through those events themselves.

The difference is one of speed and compression. Artificial Time is what happens when the production of weights from traces begins to detach from the pace of human life.
